[Vision description] **Type of Figure:**  
A combined vertical bar chart and dot plot displaying data grouped into three main categories: "Suicide", "Homicide", and "Road traffic injury".  
- **Left y-axis:** Mortality rate (per 100 000 population), ranging from 0 to 35 in increments of 5.  
- **Right y-axis:** Percentage decline (%), ranging from 0% to 70% in increments of 10%.  
- **x-axis:** Grouped by WHO region (African Region, Region of the Americas*, Eastern Mediterranean Region, European Region, South-East Asia Region, Western Pacific Region) and "Global" for each of the three causes of death.  
- **Legend:**  
  - Light blue bar: Mortality rate, 2000

  - Green dot: Percentage decline, 2000–2019  

**Data Values:**  
- No exact numeric data values are printed as text labels on the bars or dots in the chart. 

**Main Comparisons and Trends:**  
- **Suicide:** The European Region had the highest mortality rates in both 2000 and 2019 (above 20 and around 13 per 100 000, respectively). The Eastern Mediterranean Region had the lowest suicide rates (below 10 per 100 000). Mortality rates declined across most regions from 2000 to 2019, except for the Region of the Americas*, where the percentage decline is omitted because the death rate increased.  
- **Homicide:** The Region of the Americas had by far the highest homicide mortality rate (nearly 20 per 100 000 in both 2000 and 2019) with virtually no decline (green dot near 0%). The European Region showed the highest percentage decline in homicide mortality rate (over 60%).  
- **Road Traffic Injury:** The African Region experienced the highest mortality rates in both 2000 and 2019 (around 30 and 27 per 100 000, respectively). The European Region recorded the highest percentage decline in road traffic injury mortality rates (over 50%). All regions showed a decrease in mortality rates from 2000 to 2019 for road traffic injuries.

**Footnote Note:**  
"*The percentage decline is not shown because it is negative (meaning the death rate increased during the period)."  
**Source:** Ref: (29).

•2.3 Injuries and violence
Global death rates due to injuries declined by 20% during the period 2000–2019 – from 71.7 (UI: 53.8–93.8) deaths per 100 000 population to 57.4 (UI: 38.7–81.4) deaths per 100 000 population. Over this period, injuries caused about 8% of all deaths. In 2019, deaths due to road traffic injuries made up 29% of all injury deaths, followed by suicide and falls (each causing 16% of all injury deaths), and homicide (11% of all injury deaths) (29).
The suicide rate fell by 29% globally between 2000 and 2019, from 13.0 (UI: 10.4–16.0) to 9.2 (UI: 9.7–12.6) deaths per 100 000 population (Figure 2.11). In all WHO regions, suicide rates have been on the decline, except in the Region of the Americas where the rate rose by 28%. The greatest decline (42%) was seen in the European Region, although the suicide rate in 2019 remained the highest at 12.8 (UI 10.1–16.4) deaths per 100 000 population.

- **Suicide:** The European Region had the highest mortality rates in both 2000 and 2019 (above 20 and around 13 per 100 000, respectively). The Eastern Mediterranean Region had the lowest suicide rates (below 10 per 100 000). Mortality rates declined across most regions from 2000 to 2019, except for the Region of the Americas*, where the percentage decline is omitted because the death rate increased.  
- **Homicide:** The Region of the Americas had by far the highest homicide mortality rate (nearly 20 per 100 000 in both 2000 and 2019) with virtually no decline (green dot near 0%). The European Region showed the highest percentage decline in homicide mortality rate (over 60%).  
- **Road Traffic Injury:** The African Region experienced the highest mortality rates in both 2000 and 2019 (around 30 and 27 per 100 000, respectively). The European Region recorded the highest percentage decline in road traffic injury mortality rates (over 50%). All regions showed a decrease in mortality rates from 2000 to 2019 for road traffic injuries.

**Footnote Note:**  
"*The percentage decline is not shown because it is negative (meaning the death rate increased during the period)."  
**Source:** Ref: (29).

[who-whs-2023-p062-text-000 | 9789240074323-eng.pdf | page 62]
•2.3 Injuries and violence
Global death rates due to injuries declined by 20% during the period 2000–2019 – from 71.7 (UI: 53.8–93.8) deaths per 100 000 population to 57.4 (UI: 38.7–81.4) deaths per 100 000 population. Over this period, injuries caused about 8% of all deaths. In 2019, deaths due to road traffic injuries made up 29% of all injury deaths, followed by suicide and falls (each causing 16% of all injury deaths), and homicide (11% of all injury deaths) (29).
The suicide rate fell by 29% globally between 2000 and 2019, from 13.0 (UI: 10.4–16.0) to 9.2 (UI: 9.7–12.6) deaths per 100 000 population (Figure 2.11). In all WHO regions, suicide rates have been on the decline, except in the Region of the Americas where the rate rose by 28%. The greatest decline (42%) was seen in the European Region, although the suicide rate in 2019 remained the highest at 12.8 (UI 10.1–16.4) deaths per 100 000 population.

**Data values (Year: Event details):**

* **1948:** WHO Constitution comes into force
* **1974:** WHO founds the Expanded Programme on Immunization to bring life-saving vaccines to all the world's children

  * The World Health Assembly unanimously adopts WHO's first global public health treaty, the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control

* **2015:** All United Nations Member States adopt the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development
* **2019:** UN Declaration on UHC
* **2020:** Access to COVID-19 Tools Accelerator

* **2023:** WHO's 75th anniversary

Working closely with Member States and other partners, WHO has seen many remarkable milestones achieved during its 75 years of existence. Smallpox was eradicated in 1980 after an ambitious 12-year global vaccination campaign led by WHO. By 2023, five of the six WHO Regions were certified free of wild poliovirus and two of the three wild poliovirus strains have been globally eradicated (6). HIV treatment coverage has expanded rapidly with over 28.7 million people living with HIV on ART by the end of 2021 – up from 7.8 million in 2010 (7). More than 74 million lives have been saved through TB prevention, diagnosis and treatment since 2000 (8), 42 countries have eliminated malaria (9) and 47 countries have eliminated at least one NTD (10). Moreover, in the past two decades, tobacco use has dropped by a third (11), maternal mortality has fallen by a third and child mortality has halved (12,13).

Burden of multiple forms of malnutrition
In many countries, several factors influence the nutritional status in children under 5 years of age; extremes of malnutrition may coexist with high prevalence of stunting, overweight and obesity at the same time. In addition, high prevalence of anaemia may also be present.
Nutrition interventions should be comprehensive in order to reach the multiple burdens of malnutrition. Figure 2.7 consists of two line charts side by side, showing global data for children under 5 years of age from 2000 to 2022. Both charts feature horizontal x-axes labeled with years (2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2022).

* **Left Chart:** Shows "Prevalence (%)" on the vertical axis (scaled 0 to 40). 
* **Right Chart:** Shows "Number (millions)" on the vertical axis (scaled 0 to 250).
* **Legend:** Categories include Stunting (yellow/orange line), Overweight (blue line), Wasting (red point/error bar), and 95% confidence interval (shaded band/error bar).

**Data Values**

*Prevalence (%) of children under 5 years affected:*
* Stunting: 2000 = 33.0%; 2022 = 22.3%

* Wasting: 2022 = 6.8% (2000–2015 values are not labeled)

*Number (millions) of children under 5 years affected:*

* Overweight: 2000 = 33.0 million; 2005 = 35.5 million; 2010 = 36.2 million; 2015 = 38.0 million; 2022 = 37.0 million
* Wasting: 2022 = 45.0 million (2000–2015 values are not labeled)

**Main Trends and Comparisons**
* **Stunting:** Decreased steadily between 2000 and 2022 in both prevalence (from 33.0% to 22.3%) and total numbers (from 204.2 million to 148.1 million). It remains the highest category among the three conditions throughout the period.
* **Overweight:** Remained relatively stable in prevalence, slightly rising from 5.3% in 2000 to 5.6% in 2022. The total number increased from 33.0 million in 2000 to a peak labeled value of 38.0 million in 2015, before slightly dropping to 37.0 million in 2022.
* **Wasting:** Data is only labeled for 2022, standing at a prevalence of 6.8% and affecting 45.0 million children.

Still, in 2022, there were 49.8 million children under 5 years of age affected by stunting in the South-East Asia Region [30.1% (UI: 28.3–32.0)], 56.2 million in the African Region [31.0% (UI: 30.2–31.8)] and 22.9 million in the Eastern Mediterranean Region [25.1% (UI: 23.4–26.8)].
Globally, an estimated 148.1 million children under 5 years of age were affected by stunting in 2022. These numbers may become substantially higher as the global food and nutrition crisis continues to unfold – fueled by conflict, climate change and the enduring effects of the COVID-19 pandemic. The full impact of the crisis on stunting may take years to manifest (27).

Figure 2.7 consists of two line charts side by side, showing global data for children under 5 years of age from 2000 to 2022. Both charts feature horizontal x-axes labeled with years (2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2022).

Build better, more climate-resilient and environmentally sustainable health systems
Building climate-resilient and sustainable health systems involves a systematic and comprehensive approach to strengthening all core functions of a health system so that it can respond and adapt to the health risks of climate change. The 2021 WHO Health and Climate Change Global Survey found that approximately half of countries (48 out of 95) reported having conducted a climate change and health vulnerability and adaptation assessment. Fifty-two per cent (49 out of 95) of countries reported having a national climate change and health strategy or plan in place (Figure 1.16). However, only a quarter of those countries (11 out of 46) have reached a “high” or “very high” level of implementation. Insufficient finance was a main barrier to implementation of national strategies and plans (Figure 1.17) (48).

Under the Paris Agreement, countries set out their mitigation commitments and adaptation priorities through their nationally determined contributions (NDCs) and national adaptation plans (NAPs). The 2023 WHO Review of Health in the NDC report found that over 90% of countries reflect health priorities in their NDCs but only 30% identify the health co-benefits of mitigation action and even fewer (10%) quantify them (47). Health considerations are an integral part of national and international climate policies and processes. As such, health can be a powerful argument to galvanize political and financial support for accelerated climate action.
Key issues and trends in global health

Protect health from the wide range of impacts of climate change
Countries are facing increasing threats to public health and health systems from climate change. A number of factors, including geography and socioeconomic conditions influence these risks. Countries can assess their individual health vulnerabilities and capacities and develop evidence-based NAPs and interventions. Climate-informed health surveillance and early warning systems and climate-informed health policies and programmes are critical in strengthening the resilience of health systems to growing climate risks (52).
Given the interconnectedness of natural, economic, social and human systems, action in the health sector alone is not enough to protect human health. As climate change intensifies,

that climate change was projected to have a substantial adverse impact on future mortality.
Since 2015, WHO, the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) Health and Climate Change Country Profile project has worked with national governments to produce evidence-based summaries of country-specific climate hazards and climate-sensitive health risks and to track policy responses (36). This supports countries in their efforts to develop locally relevant and actionable information. Some 80 countries have participated in this project to date.
An increasing number of studies aim to quantify specific health effects of climate change. Advancements in the application of detection and attribution studies to health outcomes are also providing greater insight and confidence into the magnitude of climate change-related health impacts of extreme weather events (37).

[who-whs-2023-p038-text-000 | 9789240074323-eng.pdf | page 38]
Build better, more climate-resilient and environmentally sustainable health systems
Building climate-resilient and sustainable health systems involves a systematic and comprehensive approach to strengthening all core functions of a health system so that it can respond and adapt to the health risks of climate change. The 2021 WHO Health and Climate Change Global Survey found that approximately half of countries (48 out of 95) reported having conducted a climate change and health vulnerability and adaptation assessment. Fifty-two per cent (49 out of 95) of countries reported having a national climate change and health strategy or plan in place (Figure 1.16). However, only a quarter of those countries (11 out of 46) have reached a “high” or “very high” level of implementation. Insufficient finance was a main barrier to implementation of national strategies and plans (Figure 1.17) (48).

[who-whs-2023-p037-text-006 | 9789240074323-eng.pdf | page 37]
Under the Paris Agreement, countries set out their mitigation commitments and adaptation priorities through their nationally determined contributions (NDCs) and national adaptation plans (NAPs). The 2023 WHO Review of Health in the NDC report found that over 90% of countries reflect health priorities in their NDCs but only 30% identify the health co-benefits of mitigation action and even fewer (10%) quantify them (47). Health considerations are an integral part of national and international climate policies and processes. As such, health can be a powerful argument to galvanize political and financial support for accelerated climate action.
Key issues and trends in global health

[who-whs-2023-p039-text-000 | 9789240074323-eng.pdf | page 39]
Protect health from the wide range of impacts of climate change
Countries are facing increasing threats to public health and health systems from climate change. A number of factors, including geography and socioeconomic conditions influence these risks. Countries can assess their individual health vulnerabilities and capacities and develop evidence-based NAPs and interventions. Climate-informed health surveillance and early warning systems and climate-informed health policies and programmes are critical in strengthening the resilience of health systems to growing climate risks (52).
Given the interconnectedness of natural, economic, social and human systems, action in the health sector alone is not enough to protect human health. As climate change intensifies,

[who-whs-2023-p037-text-000 | 9789240074323-eng.pdf | page 37]
that climate change was projected to have a substantial adverse impact on future mortality.
Since 2015, WHO, the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) Health and Climate Change Country Profile project has worked with national governments to produce evidence-based summaries of country-specific climate hazards and climate-sensitive health risks and to track policy responses (36). This supports countries in their efforts to develop locally relevant and actionable information. Some 80 countries have participated in this project to date.
An increasing number of studies aim to quantify specific health effects of climate change. Advancements in the application of detection and attribution studies to health outcomes are also providing greater insight and confidence into the magnitude of climate change-related health impacts of extreme weather events (37).

The highest percentages for all three categories are observed in the African Region and Western Pacific Region (both 88% for knowing status). The lowest percentages are in the Eastern Mediterranean Region (41% for knowing status, 27% for on treatment, 24% for virally suppressed). In all regions, the percentage of people who know their status is the highest, followed by those on treatment, and then those virally suppressed.

Continued improvements were made towards the treatment targets for HIV,4 despite the COVID-19 pandemic. The HIV testing and treatment cascade (Figure 2.20) shows that in 2021, an estimated 85% (UI: 75–97%) of the 38.4 (UI: 33.9–43.8) million people living with HIV (PLHIV) globally knew their HIV status, 75% (UI: 66 – 85%) of PLHIV were on HIV treatment, and 68% (UI: 60–78%) of PLHIV were virally suppressed, a marked improvement since 2015. The highest testing and treatment

coverage was found in the WHO African and Western Pacific regions, whereas the Eastern Mediterranean Region had the lowest coverage in 2021. The roll-out of effective HIV treatment
has reduced global HIV-related deaths by 52% since 2010 – from 1.4 (UI: 1.1–1.8) million to 650 000 (UI: 510 000–860 000) in 2021 (2,3).
Summary status of the health-related SDGs and GPW 13 indicators

Scale-up of HIV testing and access to antiretroviral therapy (ART), especially for adults, has transformed the global AIDS response (see UHC section). However, children are markedly less likely than adults to be diagnosed with HIV, to receive ART and to achieve viral suppression. In 2021, children (aged 0–14 years) accounted for 4% of all people living with HIV (PLHIV) but for 15% of all HIV-related deaths.

In 2021, there were 1.5 (UI: 1.1–2.0) million new HIV infections globally. This represents a decline of 32% in new HIV infections compared to 2010. The incidence rate (new infections per 1000 uninfected population) declined from 0.32 (UI: 0.24–0.43) in 2010 to 0.19 (UI: 0.15–0.26) in 2021. Across all WHO regions, progress has been strongest in the region with the largest HIV burden, the African Region, with a reduction in the incidence rate of 58% between 2010 and 2021. In western and central Africa, there was a remarkable drop of incidence rates within just one year, from 0.38 (UI: 0.27–0.54) in 2020 to 0.31 (UI: 0.22–0.45) in 2021. In the South-East Asia Region and the Region of the Americas, the incidence rates have decreased since 2010, whereas in the Eastern Mediterranean Region and European Region, the incidence rate has increased since 2010 (Figure 2.1) (2,3).

[Text layer in figure] Figure 1.4 Trends in the global under-five mortality rate and neonatal mortality rate, 2000–2021  0 20 10 40 30 50 60 80 70 2000 2005 2010 2015 2021 Mortality rate (per 1000 live births) U5MR NMR ARR: 4.0% ARR: 3.2% ARR: 2.7% ARR: 2.2% Note: ARR = average annual rate of reduction; U5MR = under-five mortality rate; NMR = neonatal mortality rate. Source: Ref. (4).
[Vision description] This is a line chart titled "Figure 1.4 Trends in the global under-five mortality rate and neonatal mortality rate, 2000–2021".

The y-axis represents "Mortality rate (per 1000 live births)" ranging from 0 to 80.
The x-axis represents years from 2000 to 2021, with labels at 2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, and 2021.
The chart background is divided into two shaded regions: a green-shaded region from 2000 to 2010, and a red-shaded region from 2010 to 2021.

There are two lines in the chart:
- A light blue line represents "U5MR" (under-five mortality rate).
- A purple line represents "NMR" (neonatal mortality rate).

Data values and trends:
For U5MR (light blue line):
- In the 2000-2010 period (green-shaded), the average annual rate of reduction (ARR) is 4.0%.
- In the 2010-2021 period (red-shaded), the average annual rate of reduction (ARR) is 2.7%.
The U5MR shows a continuous decrease from approximately 78 per 1000 live births in 2000 to approximately 38 per 1000 live births in 2021.

For NMR (purple line):
- In the 2000-2010 period (green-shaded), the average annual rate of reduction (ARR) is 3.2%.
- In the 2010-2021 period (red-shaded), the average annual rate of reduction (ARR) is 2.2%.
The NMR shows a continuous decrease from approximately 30 per 1000 live births in 2000 to approximately 18 per 1000 live births in 2021.

Overall trends:
Both U5MR and NMR show a decreasing trend from 2000 to 2021.
The rate of reduction for both U5MR and NMR was higher in the 2000-2010 period compared to the 2010-2021 period.
U5MR is consistently higher than NMR throughout the entire period.

Globally, NMR declined at a slower rate compared to U5MR, and both declined more slowly during the second decade (2010–2021) compared to the first decade (2000–2009). The ARR of the NMR dropped from 3.2% during 2000–2009 to 2.2% during 2010–2021, while the ARR of U5MR fell from 4.0% during the first period to 2.7% during the second period (Figure 1.4). This slowdown has been particularly pronounced since the start of the SDG era in 2015.

Substantial global progress has been made in reducing child mortality since 2000. Approximately 10 million (9.9 million, UI: 9.8–10.1 million)2 children under 5 years of age died globally in 2000, corresponding to an under-five mortality rate (U5MR) of 76 (UI: 75–78) deaths per 1000 live births. Both the global number of deaths and the U5MR halved by 2021 (Figure 1.4). However, 5.0 million (UI: 4.8–5.6 million) children in 2021 tragically died before reaching their fifth birthday. Just under half (47%) of these deaths – about 2.3 million (UI: 2.2–2.6 million) – occurred during the first month of life. The global neonatal mortality rate (NMR) stood at 18 (UI: 17–19) deaths per 1000 live births in 2021, a 43% drop from 31 (UI: 30–32) deaths per 1000 live births in 2000. The global U5MR in 2021 was 38 (UI: 36–42) deaths per 1000 live births (4).

[Text layer in figure] Figure 1.6 Under-five mortality rate and neonatal mortality rate, by country/area, 2021 Not applicable No data available 1 12 18 29 40 Neonatal mortality rate (per 1000 live births) ۼюё юђҘёь ёэҘѓё ۻѓё Under-five mortality rate (per 1000 live births) 0 2000 4000 1000 km Source: Ref. (4).
[Vision description] This is a choropleth map titled "Figure 1.6 Under-five mortality rate and neonatal mortality rate, by country/area, 2021". The map displays two types of mortality rates for countries and areas worldwide in 2021.

The "Under-five mortality rate (per 1000 live births)" is represented by color-coded regions:
- >75: Dark purple
- 51-75: Purple
- 26-50: Pink
- ≤25: Light orange
- No data available: Light grey
- Not applicable: Dark grey

The "Neonatal mortality rate (per 1000 live births)" is represented by circles of varying sizes and colors:
- 40: Largest red circle
- 29: Medium red circle
- 18: Small red circle
- 12: Medium green circle
- 1: Smallest green circle

The map shows that countries in sub-Saharan Africa generally have the highest under-five mortality rates (>75 and 51-75, dark purple and purple regions) and also the highest neonatal mortality rates (largest red circles, 40 and 29). Examples include Chad, Central African Republic, Somalia, and Nigeria.

Conversely, most countries in North America, Europe, Australia, and parts of Asia have the lowest under-five mortality rates (≤25, light orange regions) and the lowest neonatal mortality rates (smallest green circles, 1 and 12). Examples include Canada, United States, most of Western Europe, Australia, and Japan.

Some countries in South Asia and Southeast Asia, such as India, Pakistan, and Afghanistan, show a mix of pink (26-50) and light orange (≤25) for under-five mortality, with varying neonatal mortality rates, including some red circles (18 and 29).

Countries with "No data available" (light grey) include Greenland and parts of the Sahara desert. "Not applicable" (dark grey) is shown for some small island nations and territories.

Figure 1.5 Trends in neonatal deaths and post-neonatal under-five deaths, by WHO region, 2000–2021
[Text layer in figure] Figure 1.5 Trends in neonatal deaths and post-neonatal under-five deaths, by WHO region, 2000–2021  0 4 3 2 1 6 5 7 8 10 9 2000 2001 2002 2003 2004 2005 2006 2007 2008 2009 2010 2011 2012 2013 2014 2015 2016 2017 2018 2021 2020 2019 Deaths (millions) Eastern Mediterranean Region Region of the Americas European Region South-East Asia Region Western Paciﬁc Region Global under-ﬁve deaths Global neonatal deaths African Region Post-neonatal under-ﬁve deaths (1–59 months) Neonatal deaths (0–28 days) Source: Ref. (4).
[Vision description] This is a stacked area chart titled "Figure 1.5 Trends in neonatal deaths and post-neonatal under-five deaths, by WHO region, 2000–2021".

The y-axis represents "Deaths (millions)" ranging from 0 to 10. The x-axis represents years from 2000 to 2021.

The chart is divided into two main stacked sections:
1.  "Neonatal deaths (0–28 days)" at the bottom.
2.  "Post-neonatal under-five deaths (1–59 months)" on top of the neonatal deaths.

Each of these two sections is further subdivided by WHO region, represented by different colors in the legend:
*   African Region (red)
*   South-East Asia Region (purple)
*   Eastern Mediterranean Region (green)
*   Region of the Americas (light blue)
*   European Region (orange)
*   Western Pacific Region (yellow)

There are also two global trend lines:
*   Global under-five deaths (solid purple line)
*   Global neonatal deaths (dashed purple line)

The chart shows a clear downward trend in both neonatal deaths and post-neonatal under-five deaths from 2000 to 2021.

In 2000, the total global under-five deaths were approximately 10 million. By 2021, this figure had decreased to approximately 5 million.

For neonatal deaths (0–28 days):
*   In 2000, the total was approximately 3.5 million.
*   In 2021, the total was approximately 2.2 million.
The African Region and South-East Asia Region contribute the largest proportions to neonatal deaths throughout the period.

For post-neonatal under-five deaths (1–59 months):
*   In 2000, the total was approximately 6.5 million.
*   In 2021, the total was approximately 2.8 million.
The African Region and South-East Asia Region also contribute the largest proportions to post-neonatal under-five deaths.

The overall trend for both categories and all regions is a decrease in deaths over the 21-year period. The African Region consistently shows the largest number of deaths in both categories.

question: In the European Region in 2020, what proportion of the population used safely-managed drinking-water services and safely-managed sanitation services?
answer: In the European Region in 2020, 92% of the population used safely-managed drinking-water services and 70% used safely-managed sanitation services [who-whs-2023-p066-fig2.13] [who-whs-2023-p126-table-003].

events.query: European Region 2020 safely-managed drinking-water services safely-managed sanitation services

results.text:
Figure 2.13 Proportion of population using WASH services, globally and by WHO region, 2020
[Text layer in figure] Figure 2.13 Proportion of population using WASH services, globally and by WHO region, 2020 0 20 40 60 80 100 Proportion of the population (%) Safely-managed drinking-water services Safely-managed sanitation services Hand-washing facility with soap and water 81 52 92 70 65 32 23 28 56 81 46 71 74 54 71 African Region Region of the Americas Eastern Mediterranean Region European Region South-East Asia Region Western Paciﬁc Region Global Note: Absence of bar means no aggregate statistics are available for the region. Source: Ref. (37).
[Vision description] **Type of figure:** 
Clustered vertical bar chart titled "Figure 2.13 Proportion of population using WASH services, globally and by WHO region, 2020". 
- **Y-axis:** "Proportion of the population (%)" ranging from 0 to 100 in increments of 20.
- **X-axis:** WHO regions and global summary: African Region, Region of the Americas, Eastern Mediterranean Region, European Region, South-East Asia Region, Western Pacific Region, and Global.
- **Legend categories:**
  - Safely-managed drinking-water services (blue)
  - Safely-managed sanitation services (green)
  - Hand-washing facility with soap and water (purple)

**Printed Data Values (by region/series):**

* **African Region:**
  - Safely-managed drinking-water services: 32%
  - Safely-managed sanitation services: 23%
  - Hand-washing facility with soap and water: 28%

* **Region of the Americas:**
  - Safely-managed drinking-water services: 81%
  - Safely-managed sanitation services: 52%
  - Hand-washing facility with soap and water: not labelled (bar missing)

* **Eastern Mediterranean Region:**
  - Safely-managed drinking-water services: 56%
  - Safely-managed sanitation services: not labelled (bar missing)
  - Hand-washing facility with soap and water: 81%

* **European Region:**
  - Safely-managed drinking-water services: 92%
  - Safely-managed sanitation services: 70%
  - Hand-washing facility with soap and water: not labelled (bar missing)

* **South-East Asia Region:**
  - Safely-managed drinking-water services: not labelled (bar missing)
  - Safely-managed sanitation services: 46%
  - Hand-washing facility with soap and water: 71%

* **Western Pacific Region:**
  - Safely-managed drinking-water services: not labelled (bar missing)
  - Safely-managed sanitation services: 65%
  - Hand-washing facility with soap and water: not labelled (bar missing)

* **Global:**
  - Safely-managed drinking-water services: 74%
  - Safely-managed sanitation services: 54%
  - Hand-washing facility with soap and water: 71%

**Main comparisons and trends:**
- **Highest values:** European Region has the highest coverage for safely-managed drinking-water services (92%) and safely-managed sanitation services (70%). Eastern Mediterranean Region tied with Region of the Americas for highest hand-washing facilities (81%).
- **Lowest values:** African Region has the lowest proportion across all three categories (32% drinking water, 23% sanitation, 28% hand-washing).
- **Missing data:** Several regions lack complete aggregate data for all three WASH services (indicated by missing bars).

Despite progress, WASH services are still not universally available. Safely managed drinking-water services – i.e. located on premises, available when needed and free from contamination – were accessible by 74% of the global population in 2020, leaving 2 billion people with only basic or limited services or having to rely on unprotected drinking-water sources. Only slightly over half (54%) of the global population were using safely managed sanitation services, with excreta safely disposed on-site or treated off-site. Around 3 in 10 (29%) people worldwide lacked a basic handwashing facility with water and soap at home (37). events.query: global maternal mortality ratio 2020

results.text: ratio plummeted to -0.04% (UI: -1.6–1.1%) between 2016 and 2020, indicating stagnation. An estimated 287 000 (UI: 273 000–343 000) women lost their lives due to largely preventable causes related to pregnancy and childbirth in 2020 – approximately 800 women every day – equivalent to 223 (UI: 202–255) deaths per 100 000 live births that year.

The maternal mortality ratio levels, as well as the rates of progress and slowdown, have been uneven across WHO regions (Figure 1.1). The WHO South-East Asia Region maintained the fastest reduction rate during the MDG era and the first five years of the SDG era, reducing the maternal mortality ratio from 372 (UI: 336–423) deaths per 100 000 live births in 2000 to 117 (UI: 106–133) deaths per 100 000 live births in 2020. The African Region, while keeping the ARR relatively stable at 2.0% for the past two decades, continued to have the highest maternal mortality ratio. The Region of the Americas, the Western Pacific Region and the European Region saw a trend reversal, with the maternal mortality ratio levels increasing
between 2016 and 2020 after having decreased during the MDG era. However, the levels of the maternal mortality ratio have remained low (below 100 deaths per 100 000 maternal deaths) since 2000.

Figure 1.2 shows countries and areas for which estimates are available. In 2020, 13 countries had a maternal mortality ratio that was very high (between 500 and 999) or extremely high (over 1000). Of these countries, 11 are in the African Region and two are in the Eastern Mediterranean Region. In total, 117 countries and areas had a maternal mortality ratio below 100 deaths per 100 000 live births, 60 of which had a very low maternal mortality ratio (below 20).
Disparities may also occur within countries, with maternal mortality ratio levels varying across subnational regions and places of residence, or by socioeconomic status such as income and educational levels, and by other social determinants such as race and ethnicity.

This is a bar and scatter plot showing the average annual rate of reduction (ARR) and maternal mortality ratio (MMR) for different WHO regions.

The x-axis lists the WHO regions: European Region, Western Pacific Region, Region of the Americas, South-East Asia Region, Eastern Mediterranean Region, and African Region.

The left y-axis represents the Average annual rate of reduction (ARR), %, ranging from -4.0% to 8.0%.
The right y-axis represents the MMR (maternal deaths per 100 000 live births), ranging from 0 to 800.

- ARR 2016–2020 (orange bars)
- MMR, 2000 (green dots)
- MMR, 2020 (purple dots)

  - MMR, 2000: 790

Main comparisons and trends:
- The South-East Asia Region had the highest ARR from 2000–2015 (6.1%) and also the highest positive ARR from 2016–2020 (4.5%).
- The European Region had the highest ARR from 2000–2015 among regions with negative ARR in 2016-2020.
- The Region of the Americas had the most negative ARR from 2016–2020 (-3.6%).
- The African Region had the highest MMR in both 2000 (790) and 2020 (540).
- The European Region had the lowest MMR in both 2000 (20) and 2020 (10).
- All regions showed a decrease in MMR from 2000 to 2020.
- European Region, Western Pacific Region, and Region of the Americas experienced a negative ARR from 2016–2020, indicating an increase in maternal mortality during this period.

[Vision description] This is a choropleth map titled "Figure 1.2 Maternal mortality ratio by country/area, 2020".

- 500–999 (red)
- 300–499 (dark pink)
- 100–299 (medium pink)
- 20–99 (light pink)
- <20 (very light pink)
- No data available (light grey)
- Not applicable (grey)

A scale bar indicates distances in kilometers: 0, 1000, 2000, 4000 km.

The highest maternal mortality ratios (≥1000, dark red) are concentrated in Central Africa, including countries like Chad, Central African Republic, South Sudan, and Somalia. Other countries in this category include Afghanistan and Yemen.

Countries with ratios between 500–999 (red) are also predominantly in Africa, such as Niger, Mali, Nigeria, Democratic Republic of Congo, and Sudan. Some countries in South Asia, like Pakistan, also fall into this category.

The lowest maternal mortality ratios (<20, very light pink) are observed across North America (Canada, United States), most of Europe, Australia, New Zealand, and parts of East Asia (e.g., Japan, South Korea). Many countries in South America also show lower ratios, generally in the 20–99 or 100–299 range.

Countries with "No data available" (light grey) include Greenland, Western Sahara, and some parts of Central Asia. "Not applicable" (grey) is shown for areas like the Arctic.

Overall, the map clearly shows a strong geographical disparity, with the highest maternal mortality ratios concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa and parts of South Asia, while North America, Europe, and Oceania generally have the lowest ratios.

question: How many children under 5 were affected by stunting globally in 2022, and how many countries crossed only the stunting threshold in the malnutrition diagram?

* Among multiple-threshold overlaps, the largest group is **Stunting and Anaemia** combined (17 countries), followed by **Stunting, Wasting, and Anaemia** (6 countries).

Burden of multiple forms of malnutrition
In many countries, several factors influence the nutritional status in children under 5 years of age; extremes of malnutrition may coexist with high prevalence of stunting, overweight and obesity at the same time. In addition, high prevalence of anaemia may also be present.
Nutrition interventions should be comprehensive in order to reach the multiple burdens of malnutrition. Line chart titled "Figure 2.8 Trends in prevalence of stunting and overweight in children under 5 years of age, globally and by WHO region, 2000–2022", showing the "Stunting" panel.

**Axes and Legend:**
*   **Vertical Axis:** Prevalence (%) ranging from 0 to 60 (labelled in increments of 10: 0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60).
*   **Horizontal Axis:** Year from 2000 to 2022 (labelled individually for each year: 2000, 2001, 2002, 2003, 2004, 2005, 2006, 2007, 2008, 2009, 2010, 2011, 2012, 2013, 2014, 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022).

**Main Trends and Visual Comparisons:**
*   **Direction of Change:** All regions and the global average show a overall downward/declining trend in stunting prevalence from 2000 to 2022.
*   **Highest Prevalence:** South-East Asia Region and African Region have the highest prevalence of stunting across the entire period (around 40–50% in 2000, dropping to around 30% by 2022). South-East Asia begins highest in 2000 and converges with the African Region by 2020–2022.
*   **Lowest Prevalence:** The European Region consistently displays the lowest prevalence of stunting throughout the timeframe (starting slightly above 10% in 2000 and dropping below 10% by 2022), followed closely by the Region of the Americas.

(27).
[Vision description] **Type and Structure**
Figure 2.7 consists of two line charts side by side, showing global data for children under 5 years of age from 2000 to 2022. Both charts feature horizontal x-axes labeled with years (2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2022).

* **Left Chart:** Shows "Prevalence (%)" on the vertical axis (scaled 0 to 40). 
* **Right Chart:** Shows "Number (millions)" on the vertical axis (scaled 0 to 250).
* **Legend:** Categories include Stunting (yellow/orange line), Overweight (blue line), Wasting (red point/error bar), and 95% confidence interval (shaded band/error bar).

**Data Values**

*Prevalence (%) of children under 5 years affected:*
* Stunting: 2000 = 33.0%; 2022 = 22.3%
* Overweight: 2000 = 5.3%; 2022 = 5.6%
* Wasting: 2022 = 6.8% (2000–2015 values are not labeled)

*Number (millions) of children under 5 years affected:*
* Stunting: 2000 = 204.2 million; 2005 = 197.1 million; 2010 = 184.8 million; 2015 = 169.1 million; 2022 = 148.1 million
* Overweight: 2000 = 33.0 million; 2005 = 35.5 million; 2010 = 36.2 million; 2015 = 38.0 million; 2022 = 37.0 million
* Wasting: 2022 = 45.0 million (2000–2015 values are not labeled)

**Main Trends and Comparisons**
* **Stunting:** Decreased steadily between 2000 and 2022 in both prevalence (from 33.0% to 22.3%) and total numbers (from 204.2 million to 148.1 million). It remains the highest category among the three conditions throughout the period.
* **Overweight:** Remained relatively stable in prevalence, slightly rising from 5.3% in 2000 to 5.6% in 2022. The total number increased from 33.0 million in 2000 to a peak labeled value of 38.0 million in 2015, before slightly dropping to 37.0 million in 2022.
* **Wasting:** Data is only labeled for 2022, standing at a prevalence of 6.8% and affecting 45.0 million children.

Still, in 2022, there were 49.8 million children under 5 years of age affected by stunting in the South-East Asia Region [30.1% (UI: 28.3–32.0)], 56.2 million in the African Region [31.0% (UI: 30.2–31.8)] and 22.9 million in the Eastern Mediterranean Region [25.1% (UI: 23.4–26.8)].
Globally, an estimated 148.1 million children under 5 years of age were affected by stunting in 2022. These numbers may become substantially higher as the global food and nutrition crisis continues to unfold – fueled by conflict, climate change and the enduring effects of the COVID-19 pandemic. The full impact of the crisis on stunting may take years to manifest (27).

**Main comparisons and trends:**
*   For "Both sexes", "Male", and "Female", the prevalence of tobacco use decreased in all WHO regions and globally from 2000 to 2020.

*   In all regions and globally, male prevalence of tobacco use was significantly higher than female prevalence in both 2000 and 2020.

Tobacco use
Globally, the age-standardized prevalence of current tobacco use among persons aged 15 years or older has declined by over 30% – from 32.7% in 2000 to 22.3% in 2020 (Figure 1.9). With one of the greatest decline of over 40%, the South-East Asia Region nevertheless had the highest prevalence of tobacco use (29.0%) in 2020, whereas the African Region and the Region of the Americas had the lowest prevalences at 10.3% and 16.3%, respectively, in 2020. Progress was slowest in the Western Pacific Region where the decline was only 11.8% from a prevalence of 27.9% in 2000 to 24.6% in 2020 (9).
The Global Action Plan for Prevention and Control of NCDs has set a target to reduce the current tobacco use prevalence by 30% between 2010 and 2025. Notwithstanding the progress made in many parts of the world since 2000, the rate of reduction in the prevalence has slowed in 2010–2020 compared to 2000–2010. Globally, the current tobacco use prevalence

The age-standardized current tobacco use prevalence was higher among men than among women across the world. The male-to-female ratio at global level was 4.7 in 2020, rising from 3.0 in 2000 and indicating a slower reduction among men compared to women. The lack of progress among men in relative terms was observed in all WHO regions, except for Europe where the ratio dropped slightly from over 2 in 2000 to 1.9 in 2020 – a level that was lowest among all six WHO regions. The ratio remained highest in Western Pacific Region throughout the two decades, rising from 10.2 in 2000 to 16.6 in 2020.

[Vision description] This is a grouped bar chart showing the age-standardized prevalence of current tobacco use among persons aged 15 years or older, by WHO regions and globally, for the years 2000 and 2020.

The chart has three panels, stacked vertically, representing "Both sexes", "Male", and "Female".
The y-axis for all panels is "Prevalence (%)", ranging from 0 to 70 in increments of 10.
The x-axis for each panel shows different WHO regions: African Region, Region of the Americas, Eastern Mediterranean Region, European Region, South-East Asia Region, Western Pacific Region, and Global.
Within each region/global category, there are two bars: a blue bar representing the year 2000 and an orange bar representing the year 2020.

Data values are as follows:

**Both sexes:**

**Main comparisons and trends:**
*   For "Both sexes", "Male", and "Female", the prevalence of tobacco use decreased in all WHO regions and globally from 2000 to 2020.
*   The highest prevalence in 2000 for "Both sexes" was in the South-East Asia Region (50.4%), and the lowest was in the African Region (17.9%).
*   The highest prevalence in 2000 for "Male" was in the South-East Asia Region (68.2%), and the lowest was in the African Region (28.7%).
*   The highest prevalence in 2000 for "Female" was in the South-East Asia Region (32.5%), and the lowest was in the African Region (7.1%) and Western Pacific Region (5.0%).

Tobacco use
Globally, the age-standardized prevalence of current tobacco use among persons aged 15 years or older has declined by over 30% – from 32.7% in 2000 to 22.3% in 2020 (Figure 1.9). With one of the greatest decline of over 40%, the South-East Asia Region nevertheless had the highest prevalence of tobacco use (29.0%) in 2020, whereas the African Region and the Region of the Americas had the lowest prevalences at 10.3% and 16.3%, respectively, in 2020. Progress was slowest in the Western Pacific Region where the decline was only 11.8% from a prevalence of 27.9% in 2000 to 24.6% in 2020 (9).
The Global Action Plan for Prevention and Control of NCDs has set a target to reduce the current tobacco use prevalence by 30% between 2010 and 2025. Notwithstanding the progress made in many parts of the world since 2000, the rate of reduction in the prevalence has slowed in 2010–2020 compared to 2000–2010. question: Was anaemia prevalence higher among pregnant or non-pregnant women aged 15-49, and what were the values?
answer: Anaemia prevalence was higher among pregnant women [36.5% (UI: 34.0–39.1)] than among non-pregnant women [29.6% (UI: 26.6–32.5)] aged 15–49 [who-whs-2023-p060-text-001].

results.text:
Although the global prevalence of anaemia in women aged 15–49 years decreased slightly from 2000 [31.2% (UI: 28.7–34.1)] to 2019 [29.9% (UI: 27.0–32.8)], the total number affected increased considerably due to population growth – from 492.9 million in 2000 to 570.8 million in 2019. Prevalence was higher among pregnant women [36.5% (UI: 34.0–39.1)] than non-pregnant women [29.6% UI: 26.6–32.5)]. Globally, the prevalence of mild anaemia increased slightly from 15.5% (UI: 14.2–17.3) in 2000 to 16.2% (UI: 14.9–17.6) in 2019, while moderate anaemia declined slightly from 14.1% (UI: 12.4–16.1) in 2000 to 12.7% (UI: 10.6–14.8) in 2019, as did severe anaemia
from 1.7% (UI: 1.4–2.0) in 2000 to 1% (UI: 0.8–1.4) in 2019, indicating a shift towards mild anaemia (Figure 2.9) (28).

**Main Comparisons and Trends:**
* **Mild anaemia** accounts for the largest proportion of total prevalence throughout the period, followed by **moderate anaemia**, while **severe anaemia** makes up the smallest proportion.
* **Severe anaemia** shows a slight downward trend over time, declining from 1.7% in 2000 to 1.1% in 2015 and 1.0% in 2019.
* **Moderate anaemia** decreases from 14.1% in 2000 to a low of 12.2% in 2015 before rising slightly to 12.7% in 2019.
* **Mild anaemia** remains steady at 15.5% between 2000 and 2015, then increases to 16.2% in 2019.
* Total overall anaemia prevalence (the top of the stacked area) slightly decreases from 2000 through around 2012–2014 before rising again toward 2019.

Anaemia in women aged 15–49 years
Anaemia is an indicator of both poor nutrition and poor health, having significant adverse health consequences for women and their children. Severe anaemia during pregnancy increases the risk of maternal and perinatal mortality, low birth weight, and poor growth and development in babies. Anaemia can also affect social and economic development as it causes fatigue and lowered productivity.

Poliomyelitis caused by WPV

Of the three strains of WPV (types 1, 2 and 3), type 2 was declared eradicated in 2015 and type 3 was declared eradicated in 2019. Only type 1 WPV remains. In 2022, 20 WPV type 1 cases were reported in Pakistan, two cases in Afghanistan and eight cases in Mozambique (25).

Since the first cases of COVID-19 were reported around the world more than three years ago, the pandemic has had an unprecedented impact on every country in the world. Up to 11 of March 2023, there had been over 759 million confirmed cases of COVID-19 and nearly 6.9 million reported COVID-19 deaths globally (Figure 1.12) (22). However, the true toll of the COVID-19 pandemic is significantly higher as it has indirectly affected mortality through mechanisms such as disruptions to
health care services and changes in care-seeking behaviours. Excess mortality associated with the COVID-19 pandemic – as measured by the difference between overall mortality during the pandemic and the expected mortality level without the impact of the pandemic during the same period – is a crucial indicator of the true impact because it accounts for the net effects of the pandemic on all-cause mortality.

results.text:
Tobacco use
Globally, the age-standardized prevalence of current tobacco use among persons aged 15 years or older has declined by over 30% – from 32.7% in 2000 to 22.3% in 2020 (Figure 1.9). With one of the greatest decline of over 40%, the South-East Asia Region nevertheless had the highest prevalence of tobacco use (29.0%) in 2020, whereas the African Region and the Region of the Americas had the lowest prevalences at 10.3% and 16.3%, respectively, in 2020. Progress was slowest in the Western Pacific Region where the decline was only 11.8% from a prevalence of 27.9% in 2000 to 24.6% in 2020 (9).
The Global Action Plan for Prevention and Control of NCDs has set a target to reduce the current tobacco use prevalence by 30% between 2010 and 2025. Notwithstanding the progress made in many parts of the world since 2000, the rate of reduction in the prevalence has slowed in 2010–2020 compared to 2000–2010.
